clue.text: Aspiration shunned by Arden sun-lovers

explanation.surface: A literary note on what the exiles in Shakespeare's Forest of Arden turn their backs on.
explanation.walkthrough: In As You Like It the song 'Under the greenwood tree' welcomes one 'Who doth ambition shun, And loves to live i' the sun': the forest exiles are the sun-lovers.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses name the drive to get on in the world: a synonym for aspiration, and the very thing the Arden song says its sun-loving singers reject.

clue.text: Out of doors to the Italian wall-painting

parts.note: Italian al means to the, or in the
a fresco is painted on wet plaster on a wall

explanation.surface: Moving outdoors in the Italian way, with a mural for company.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian phrase, meaning in the fresh air, is used in English for outdoor activity.

clue.text: He got the measure of criminals

definitions.text: He got the measure of criminals

parts.words: He got the measure of criminals
parts.note: got the measure of means understood, but here literally measured: the French police officer who identified offenders by body measurements

explanation.walkthrough: Alphonse Bertillon devised anthropometry, a system for identifying criminals by recording body measurements, so he literally took their measure.
explanation.definitionFit: The French criminologist built an identification system out of measurements of offenders' bodies.

clue.text: Rochester's field

parts.note: Mr Rochester's house in Jane Eyre is a Hall whose name is this word joined to field, so his field is the first half of it

explanation.walkthrough: Rochester could be the Kent city; it is Mr Rochester of Jane Eyre, whose home is Thornfield Hall: the word that goes with 'field' there.
explanation.definitionFit: Mr Rochester's house in Charlotte Brontë's novel is named with this word before 'field'.

clue.text: Stanzas about avocets

indicators.note: about means around or astir, so the bird's letters are moved around

explanation.surface: A poet's stanzas written about wading birds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' looks like 'on the subject of'; it signals the rearrangement of AVOCETS.
explanation.definitionFit: An octave in verse is a stanza or group of eight lines, as in the opening of a sonnet.

clue.text: With added zest

parts.note: zest here is the tang of seasoning: food given extra flavour from pepper, cinnamon and the like

explanation.definitionFit: Food that has been seasoned with aromatic flavourings has had zest added to it.

clue.text: Transport for Anchises

parts.note: in the Aeneid Aeneas carries his old father Anchises out of burning Troy on his shoulders

explanation.walkthrough: In Virgil's Aeneid, Aeneas escapes burning Troy carrying his father Anchises on his back.
explanation.definitionFit: Being carried on someone's shoulders or back, as Aeneas carried his father, is a piggyback ride.

clue.text: Taffy on all fours ?

parts.note: Taffy is an old nickname for a Welshman, so a Welshman on four legs is the short-legged Welsh dog

explanation.walkthrough: 'Taffy' looks like toffee; it is a nickname for a Welshman. A Welsh creature on four legs is the Welsh breed of dog.
explanation.definitionFit: The short-legged herding dog originated in Wales, so it is a four-legged Welsh native.

clue.text: "Days that are over, that are done " (Swinburne)

definitions.text: Days that are over, that are done

parts.words: Days that are over, that are done
parts.note: a line from Swinburne with a gap; the missing word pairs with days that have passed, as visions of sleep

explanation.walkthrough: The line is Swinburne's: 'Days that are over, dreams that are done'; supply the missing plural noun.
explanation.definitionFit: The gap in the quoted line takes the plural noun for visions seen in sleep.

clue.text: Alien fruit in a hand of bananas

indicators.note: in tells you the answer is held inside the run of letters that follows

explanation.surface: A strange fruit spotted among a bunch of bananas.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'hand' is a bunch of bananas. 'Alien' means foreign: the word is the French and other European name for the pineapple.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the foreign, chiefly French, word for the pineapple, so a fruit with an alien name.

clue.text: What Myosotis begs not to be

definitions.text: What Myosotis begs not to be

parts.words: What Myosotis begs not to be
parts.note: Myosotis is the botanical name of the forget-me-not, whose common name is a plea to be remembered

explanation.walkthrough: Myosotis is the Latin genus name of the small blue flower called forget-me-not; its English name is a request, so the clue asks what the flower begs not to be.
explanation.definitionFit: A flower named 'forget-me-not' pleads not to slip from memory, i.e. not to be left unremembered.

clue.text: Round about 50 she would be very round!

indicators.note: the clue says that if this woman were wrapped round the Roman fifty she would become the round word, so take that numeral back out

parts.note: a circle is the roundest shape of all
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: A remark that a woman approaching fifty is getting decidedly plump.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'Round about 50' as an instruction: put the answer round L and you get CIRCLE. Working back, CIRCLE with its L taken out leaves the enchantress of the Odyssey.
explanation.definitionFit: Circe is the sorceress of Homer's Odyssey who turned Odysseus's crew into swine, so a woman.

clue.text: Not that this style was woolly

definitions.text: Not that this style was woolly

parts.words: Not that this style was woolly
parts.note: Charles Lamb wrote his essays as Elia; a lamb is woolly, but his prose style was not

explanation.walkthrough: The scan shows 'Nct', a damaged 'Not'. Charles Lamb signed his Essays as Elia, so his manner is Elian; the clue says that though he was a Lamb, his style was not woolly.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective formed from Lamb's pen name Elia describes the manner of his essays.

clue.text: From which one got sacking

parts.note: sacking reads as coarse cloth but means plundering, the work of the Germanic tribe that sacked Rome in 455

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sacking' looks like hessian cloth; it is the looting of a city. The Vandals sacked Rome in AD 455 and gave their name to wanton destruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Wanton destruction is named after the Vandals, the tribe whose sack of Rome became a byword for plunder.

clue.text: Victory fliers in rainbow formation

explanation.surface: A flypast in triumph, the planes trailing smoke in rainbow stripes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fliers' suggests aircraft but means flags that fly: a ship or regiment flies its colours in triumph.
explanation.definitionFit: Flags hoisted in triumph are a unit's standards, and a rainbow is made up of the spectrum's hues.

clue.text: Their saplings grown thus are fabulous

definitions.text: Their saplings grown thus are fabulous

parts.words: Their saplings grown thus are fabulous
parts.note: saplings that grow up become trees; this Javan tree is fabulous in that legends made it poison everything around it

explanation.walkthrough: The upas of Java was fabled to poison everything near it. Split 4-5, the answer also reads 'up as trees', which is how saplings grow.
explanation.definitionFit: The Javan upas was fabled to kill all life nearby, and its young plants grow up into these trees.

clue.text: Bunk ?

parts.note: a bunk is a sailor's berth aboard ship, a bed at sea; read as two words it also names the ocean floor

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bunk' suggests nonsense or a narrow bed; split the answer 3-3 and a ship's bunk is a bed at sea, while the whole is the floor of the ocean.
explanation.definitionFit: A berth on board ship is literally a bed used at sea, and the hyphenated phrase is the ocean floor.

clue.text: Teens date — what, with no teeth ?

indicators.note: what, said in surprise, tells you the letters before it are to be jumbled

parts.note: the two words supply the nine letters to be rearranged, taken as written

explanation.surface: Teenagers on a date, who turn out to be toothless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'what' signals rearranging TEENS DATE. Edentates are mammals such as anteaters and sloths that lack front teeth or all teeth.
explanation.definitionFit: Edentate mammals such as anteaters and sloths are toothless or nearly so.

clue.text: Liquorice helping to make the world !

explanation.surface: Sweets offered round, with an exclamation that it takes all kinds to make a world.
explanation.walkthrough: Liquorice Allsorts are a British mixed sweet; the proverb 'it takes all sorts to make a world' gives the second sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A helping of liquorice sweets is the mixed bag of that name, and the proverb says all kinds of people are needed to make up the world.

clue.text: " But a bird's weight can break the — tree ' (Browning)

definitions.text: But a bird's weight can break the — tree

parts.words: But a bird's weight can break the — tree
parts.note: a line from Robert Browning, where the missing word describes a sapling so young a bird could snap it

explanation.walkthrough: Fill the gap in Browning's line; the missing word describes a tree in its earliest growth.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective here means newly begun and very young, like a baby, fitting a sapling too frail for a bird's weight.

clue.text: "Fishes that in the deep Know no such liberty " (Lovelace)

definitions.text: Fishes that in the deep Know no such liberty

parts.words: Fishes that in the deep Know no such liberty
parts.note: a line from Richard Lovelace's To Althea, from Prison, with the verb for drinking left out

explanation.walkthrough: Lovelace wrote 'Fishes that tipple in the deep Know no such liberty'; supply the missing verb meaning to drink.
explanation.definitionFit: The gap takes a verb meaning to drink, used by Lovelace of fishes in the sea.

clue.text: Its content to be black and/or blue

definitions.text: Its content to be black and/or blue

parts.words: Its content to be black and/or blue
parts.note: content reads as contented, as of a person happy to be bruised, but means what is held: writing fluid in black or blue

explanation.walkthrough: 'black and/or blue' suggests bruising and 'content' suggests contentment; the thing described is a desk pot whose contents, ink, come in black or blue.
explanation.definitionFit: A desk pot holding writing fluid has black or blue ink as its contents.

clue.text: Theology that is nicer for peace-lovers

indicators.note: made over for peace-lovers, the letters are reshaped into the name of their own theology

explanation.surface: A kind of theology described as more agreeable for those who love peace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for peace-lovers' signals rearranging IS NICER, and also hints at the meaning: irenics is theology aimed at peace among churches.
explanation.definitionFit: Irenics is the branch of theology that seeks reconciliation and unity between Christian churches.

clue.text: The compiler's shape? Let us hope not!

definitions.text: The compiler's shape? Let us hope not!

parts.words: The compiler's shape? Let us hope not
parts.note: a crossword grid has four equal sides, but the same word means stodgy and old-fashioned, which no setter wants to be

explanation.walkthrough: The grid the setter works in is this shape, but the word also means conventional and dull, which we hope he is not.
explanation.definitionFit: A crossword grid is foursquare, and the same word is slang for someone stuffy and old-fashioned.

clue.text: Time to give us a tune, Quilp

indicators.note: Quilp is asked to perform, so the letters of tune and his name are played over in a new order

explanation.surface: Someone tells Dickens's dwarf Quilp it is his turn to sing.
explanation.walkthrough: Quilp is the villainous dwarf of Dickens's The Old Curiosity Shop. 'give us a' tells you to rework TUNE and QUILP into a new order.
explanation.definitionFit: Quintuple time is a musical metre of five beats to the bar, so the word names a kind of musical time.

clue.text: Flanking by the Trojans ?

parts.note: flanking reads as a military move but means relating to the flank or hip; Ilium is the old name of Troy

explanation.walkthrough: 'Flanking' suggests an attack on the side; the word means of the flank or hip bone, and also reads as 'of Ilium', the Latin name for Troy.
explanation.definitionFit: The anatomical adjective refers to the ilium or hip region, and it also can mean belonging to Ilium, Troy.

clue.text: Miss at Highbury ?

parts.note: Highbury is the village of Jane Austen's Emma, where a talkative spinster is known by her surname with Miss

explanation.walkthrough: Highbury suggests the London football ground; here it is the village in Austen's Emma, home of the garrulous spinster Miss Bates.
explanation.definitionFit: The chattering unmarried lady of Austen's Emma, living in Highbury, is addressed by this surname.

clue.text: Papal letter or note

explanation.surface: A letter from the Pope, or perhaps just a short note.
explanation.definitionFit: A brief is a short papal letter, for which this is an old word, and in music it is a note worth two semibreves.

clue.text: She has left the fort, altogether blue

annotationWithheld.clue: She has left the fort, altogether blue

clue.text: Farewell the square variety of sheep?

explanation.surface: A wartime goodbye to a London square, oddly followed by a question about livestock.
explanation.walkthrough: The music-hall song 'It's a Long Way to Tipperary' runs 'Goodbye Piccadilly, farewell Leicester Square'; Leicester Square is in London's West End. The Leicester is also a long-woolled English sheep.
explanation.definitionFit: The song names a West End square bid goodbye, and the same place name is an English breed of long-wool sheep.

clue.text: Not that the Budget is likely to do this to it !

definitions.text: Not that the Budget is likely to do this to it !

parts.words: Not that the Budget is likely to do this to it
parts.note: the word is both a duty on goods and a verb meaning to cut out, so the Chancellor will hardly cut out the duty

explanation.walkthrough: The answer is both a tax on home goods and a verb meaning cut out; the Budget is the Chancellor's yearly tax statement, which will hardly remove so useful a duty.
explanation.definitionFit: A duty levied on goods shares its spelling with a verb meaning to cut away, which the Budget would never do to that duty.

clue.text: Rates like taxes, we hear

indicators.note: the phrase is said out loud and the letters entered are a word spelt differently

parts.note: as means like, and cesses are taxes or levies

explanation.surface: Local rates, someone remarks, are much the same thing as taxes.
explanation.walkthrough: A cess is an old word for a tax; 'as cesses' spoken sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To rate something is to judge its value, which is to evaluate it.
